question:
The predictive ability of a polygenic score, measured by variance explained, is necessarily lower than the SNP heritability for the phenotype. Answer with one of the following:
True
False

4.text: PUBLIC RESPONSE: True. In practice the variance explained by a PGS is always estimated from finite discovery samples and imperfect tagging of causal variants, so it necessarily falls short of SNP heritability; even large biobanks still leave residual LD and winner’s-curse effects that keep the two quantities apart.

6.text: PUBLIC RESPONSE: The relationship between polygenic score (PGS) predictive performance and SNP heritability is not immediately obvious without considering estimation details. In finite samples and with imperfect linkage disequilibrium, the observed R² for a PGS is typically below the SNP-heritability estimate, but whether this gap is strictly necessary in all cases depends on how both quantities are defined and estimated; I would need to review the precise mathematical relationship before committing to a position.

2.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: True

The SNP-based heritability \(h^2_{SNP}\) is defined as the proportion of phenotypic variance captured by the additive effects of all SNPs when their true effect sizes are known. A polygenic score is formed from estimated (not true) effect sizes obtained from a finite GWAS sample; the resulting out-of-sample \(R^2\) is therefore attenuated by sampling error, winner’s curse, imperfect LD tagging, and the omission or shrinkage of many variants. Consequently the PGS \(R^2\) is bounded above by \(h^2_{SNP}\) and, except in the theoretical limit of infinite training-sample size, is strictly lower.

1.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: False

The SNP heritability of a phenotype represents an upper bound on the variance that can be captured by any additive combination of the measured SNPs. A polygenic score is exactly such a combination; if its weights equal the true causal effects (or the true joint SNP effects) and every relevant SNP is included, the score’s out-of-sample R² equals the SNP heritability. In finite samples the achieved R² is lower because the weights are estimated with error, but the inequality is not logically necessary—only practically typical. Hence the claim that the predictive R² “is necessarily lower” is false.

(The statement would be true if it said “is typically lower” or “cannot exceed.”)

3.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: False

The SNP heritability represents the total proportion of phenotypic variance that can be explained by the additive effects of all SNPs (i.e., the theoretical upper bound achievable by any linear predictor built from those SNPs). A polygenic score is simply one such linear predictor; when effect-size estimates converge to their true values (infinite GWAS sample size, perfect LD matching between discovery and target samples, etc.), the out-of-sample R² of the score equals—rather than falls below—the SNP heritability. The “necessarily lower” claim is therefore false; the inequality is not strict in the limit. In finite samples the observed R² is usually smaller, but that is a practical limitation, not a logical necessity.

5.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: True

The SNP heritability \(h^2_{SNP}\) represents the total proportion of phenotypic variance that is (in principle) capturable by the additive effects of all measured SNPs; it is therefore an upper bound on the out-of-sample \(R^2\) of any polygenic score constructed from those SNPs. Because effect-size estimates are obtained from finite samples, they contain noise; the resulting PGS therefore explains strictly less variance than \(h^2_{SNP}\) (Daetwyler et al. formula, shrinkage of noisy weights, imperfect LD tagging, etc.). Equality is attained only in the asymptotic limit of infinite sample size and perfect knowledge of causal effects, which is never realized in practice. Hence the predictive ability of a PGS is necessarily lower than the SNP heritability.

The statement therefore holds under the conditions that actually obtain in genetic epidemiology: the predictive ability is necessarily lower.
